vt35_inti_and_the_andes.topic: Inti, the Coricancha, Inti Raymi, the Punchao, Taki Onqoy and the sun in Andean Christianity

claims.text: Coricancha in Cusco was dedicated to Inti; its walls were covered in sheets of gold; in 1533, when the Spanish demanded a gold ransom for Atahualpa, most of the gold was collected from the Coricancha

The Dominicans built the church and convent of Santo Domingo on the site; construction took most of a century; the present building dates from after the 1650 earthquake; four rooms of the Inca temple survive within the convent

Inti Raymi was the Inca new-year festival of the sun at the June solstice, credited to Pachacuti; the last held with the Inca ruler present is dated to 1535 in popular accounts; Garcilaso de la Vega described it
Viceroy Francisco de Toledo in 1572 prohibited ceremonies associated with the Inca cult, Inti Raymi among them (Infobae 2026)
Revived in 1944 as a theatrical reconstruction by Humberto Vidal Unda and Faustino Espinoza Navarro, based largely on Garcilaso; staged at Sacsayhuamán on 24 June
Dean (Duke 1999): Corpus Christi in colonial Cuzco marked 'the triumph of Christian orthodoxy over the imperial Inka patron (the Sun)'
Smarthistory: Corpus Christi coincided with the Inka solstice celebration of Inti Raymi; Cusco Corpus Christi series of 18 canvases, 16 survive

Taki Onqoy arose in the 1560s around Huamanga; Luis de Olvera claimed in 1577 he discovered and corrected it in 1564; leaders said revived huacas would defeat the God of the Christians and send illness to the Spaniards

Cristóbal de Albornoz led the suppression; penalties included public shaming, shaving, whipping, forced labour, exile; women confined in convents; kurakas fined; leaders taken to Cusco to renounce; Olvera claimed destroying 700 huacas and over 8,000 idols
Varón and Guibovich argue Albornoz exaggerated the movement's spread in his 1570 probanza; it was local to parts of Ayacucho, Huancavelica, Apurímac

Toledo ordered the attack on Vilcabamba; Túpac Amaru captured 1572 and executed in Cusco 24 September 1572; clerics pleaded for him; Philip II disapproved; the Spanish seized the Punchao, a gold image holding the hearts of dead Inca kings

Julien 2002: Toledo took the Punchao to Spain in 1581; after his death in 1582 the Council of the Indies seized items; a gold idol appears in the inventory after Philip II's death in 1598, possibly kept in Madrid's Casa del Tesoro into the early 1600s; Wikipedia says the sacred items were destroyed
The Willaq Umu were the high priests of the Sun, usually brothers of the Sapa Inca; Villac Umu joined Almagro's 1535 Chile expedition and defected back to Cusco to aid the uprising

UNESCO 2011: Qoyllurit'i pilgrimage combines Catholicism and worship of pre-Hispanic nature deities; begins 58 days after Easter; about a hundred dances; procession to Tayancani to greet the first rays of sunlight

vt35_mexico_and_the_maya.topic: Huitzilopochtli, Tonatiuh, the Templo Mayor and Sun Stone, Maya sun god, codices and survivals

claims.text: Huitzilopochtli: solar and war deity, patron of the Mexica; Coatepec myth read as sun defeating moon (Coyolxauhqui) and stars (Centzon Huitznahua); tribute/sacrifice as sustenance for the sun; red south shrine of the Templo Mayor
Huitzilopochtli's image: reportedly rescued from destruction, resurfaced in the 1530s in Bishop Zumárraga's investigation, then lost
Tonatiuh: daytime sun deity, the Fifth Sun, calendar name 4 Movement; Teotihuacan myth of Nanahuatzin's self-sacrifice (Sahagún); journey sustained by daily human sacrifice

Templo Mayor dedicated to Huitzilopochtli and Tlaloc; almost totally destroyed by the Spanish in 1521; Motolinía records a feast when the sun stood in the middle of the temple, at the equinox; rediscovered 21 February 1978 by CFE workers (Coyolxauhqui disk); excavated 1978-82 under Eduardo Matos Moctezuma

Metropolitan Cathedral: conquistadors built a church on the site using stones of the destroyed temple of Huitzilopochtli; present cathedral begun 1573 around the existing church, completed 1813, on top of the former sacred precinct

Sun Stone carved c.1502-1521; central face Tonatiuh or Tlaltecuhtli (disputed); not a functioning calendar, possibly temalacatl; Archbishop Alonso de Montúfar ordered it buried per Diego Durán so the memory of sacrifice would be lost; found 17 December 1790; mounted on cathedral west tower 2 July 1791 to 1885; National Museum of Anthropology since 1964
Huei tzompantli: over 600 skulls found by INAH by December 2020; built c.1486-1502 under Ahuitzotl; 1487 figure of 20,000 sacrificed is disputed
Kinich Ahau (God G) the Yucatec and Lacandon sun god; K'inich a Classic royal title ('sun-eyed'); Landa says patron of one of four year-bearers; Lacandon narrative of Kinich Ahau ending the world

Four Maya codices survive; Dresden's tables track eclipses, equinoxes, solstices, Venus and Mars; predicted solar eclipses for 33 years in the 8th century; Landa ordered many destroyed July 1562 ('burned them all'); Maya Codex of Mexico authenticated by INAH 2018

Codex Borgia: pre-Columbian central Mexican tonalpohualli manuscript; via Giustiniani to Cardinal Stefano Borgia; to Propaganda Fide; Vatican Apostolic Library since 1902, digitised; depicts Tonatiuh receiving offerings, Venus pages
Zumárraga received apostolic inquisitor powers 1535, did not set up a tribunal, but indicted Don Carlos Ometochtzin of Texcoco for reverting to idolatry and handed him to the secular courts
Chamula Tzotzil Maya: Christ and Sun merged as Our Father Sun/Christ; Virgin, Moon, Earth merged as Our Mother; Gossen's Four Creations texts 'Of Our Father Sun in Heaven'
Voladores ritual, UNESCO 2009: fertility ceremony, respect for and harmony with natural and spiritual worlds, especially Totonac in Veracruz
Study of 41 Jesuit mission churches in NW New Spain found no clear solar orientation pattern; few face the eastern solar range
